PARALYSED?

There is something in that phrase—"the winter of our discontent." The word winter suggests bleakness and dreariness and of course coldness. There is in it the distinct call to effort—to the physical as well as the spiritual or intellectual sides of our natures. December is well upon us with the distinct, remindder of the necessity to see to such mundane things as coal, and woolens! Societies who cater for the indoor needs of their members are, as a rule, well on with their arranged programme by this time of the year. If we are right in our surmise some sort of paralysis seems to have set in. We have not yet given up hope that are long those University Extension. Lectures will be as common as they will be an acceptable feature of our everyday life. The Cathedral Chaplain suggests that we are apt to take more interest in our race meetings than we do in our University. There is half a truth in the suggestion—not a whole one; but, in idiomatic parlance "it is up to" the University to take some interest in the people who are willing to take some interest in it, if the way—is only shown. So far the University remains a "lighthouse." We should like it to be known as "the lecture house" and to do something to lighten Hongkong's winter discontent of intellectual dulness. The Helena May Institute has nobly done its share, in the past, in catering for Off mind's pleasure. There we suggest there seems to be here also, a kind of rigor mortis? In the past there was something known as The Odd Volumes Society. It dehed and

less, in its time settled many affairs of interest. As a means of the British community kindling a little understanding amongst its own members, what is to be said against the idea of a Parliamentary Debating Society free and independent from the labels of this and that society and this and that denomination of religion? We could do with some society that would take to its bosom the better type of professional entertainer who visits our often seemingly inhospitable shores. Most of us are one-sided enthusiasts, seeing no good in any but our own pursuits, hobbies, and likings. A little of the Bobbie Burns gift and we would see ourselves as we really are. Christians may be absolutely certain the necessity there is in the place to create a higher, Saner and more Christian public opinion. We are quite certain there is a need to create a higher and Saner intellectual opinion. The strike and boycott paralysed trade. Have they paralysed winter intellectual effort?

PLUCKY BOY.
DEFENDS EMPLOYER'S PROPERTY.
A COURT SEQUEL

The plucky action of a boy who when'threatened by armed robbers who were after his employer's safe, rushed away, gave the alarm and headed the chased to the appearance at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday of a man who is alleged to be one of the robbers.
The attempted "robbery took place at a Chinese shipyard at Cheung Sha Wan.
In his evidence, the boy, in answer to questions by the Bench, said that the prisoner discharged two rounds from a revolver during the chase. The revolver, which was found the following day, was produced and showed no signs of having been fired although the cartridges were marked.
The case was adjourned.

A Nursery Catalogue is probably the last place in the world in which to look for fine
spirited writing. The illustrations may be coloured, but not necesarily the descriptions. But here is an exception taken from a recent issue of a Home paper. Nurseryman's Catalogue:—

Next to the Rose, there is nothing that can equal the Psalmy for regal splendour. It is a luxurious flower, putting one in mind of quantities of volvety rose petals brought together to form a single majestic bloom. Folk who grow a few old-fashioned Psalms—huge bushes occupying several square yards of ground, which seldom produce more than two or three second or third-rate flowers—have simply no idea what our Psalms, which have been selected from the finest varieties in the world, are like The delicious fragrance of these Psalms together with their splendid form and colour, make them absolutely irresistible.
Seelandia. If flowers can be judged by the same standards as feminine beauty, it

is to this exquisite representative of the Larkspur family that the prize should go. Words could never be found to faithfully portray its delicate loveliness or perfect grace of form. The broad spikes tapering towards the top are sheathed with parma violet flowers, tinted sky blue. In the centre of each petal is a small dark eye. A valuable late-flowering variety.
Jade. Tse, Kong said to Kong-Feu-Tse:
"Dare I ask you why wise men value jade and scorn the houen stone? Is it because jade is rare and the houen stone is very common?"

"If jade is highly valued it is because, since very olden times, the wise have likened it to virtue. For them, the polish and the brilliancy of jade represent the whole of purity; its perfect compactness and its extreme hardness represent the sureness of the intelligence; its angles which do not cut, although they seem sharpest represent justice; the pure and prolonged sound which it gives forth when one strikes it, represents music.

"Its colour represents loyalty: its interior flaws; always showing themselves through the transparency, call to mind sincerity; its iridescent brightness represents the heaven; its admirable substance, born of mountain and of water, represents the earth. Cut in kouy or in tchang, to be used alone without ornamentation, it represents chastity. The price which all the world attaches to it, represents the truth: To support these comparisons, the Book of Verse says: When I think of a wise man, his merits appear to me like jade, and that is why the wise set so great store by jade."
—Le Lyjn. Translated from the Chinese by Toussaint and Joerissen.

ROUND ABOUT A MAORI VILLAGE

But though the Terraces are gone, the region to which they brought renown is still richly endowed enough with attractions to draw visitors from the other end of the globe. For its hot geysers and springs are repeatedly in action; it is the home of thousands of Maoris who still cling to many of the customs and superstitions of their forefathers; and it boasts of the modern town of Rotorua. The most interesting Maori village is Whakarewarewa, which is conveniently shortened to Whaka. It is only two miles away from Rotorua, and coaches ply frequently during the day between town and village.

A southward journey of seven hours by rail from Auckland brings you to a region unparalleled for its array of weird wonders. It is a region of geysers and thermal springs, of boiling fountains and bubbling pools, of menacing craters and hot fissured soil, set amidst placid lakes and frowning mountains. It is the region where once existed the eighth wonder of the world; the Pink and White Terracas of Rotomahana, those beautiful, spacious and symmetrical alabaster formations that drew "throngs of admirers from all parts of the world. The Terraces... now lie buried beneath the water of the Lake Rotomahana."

Whaka presents a strange and eerie scene, probably without equal throughout the world. There are clusters of wooden huts built on the sandy or stony soil, in which the natives live, clad in modern garb, and all around are geysers and hot springs from which snow-white clouds of vapour arise or jets of boiling water shoot aloft, whilst the air reeks of sulphur. Every geyser has its own particular characteristics and significant name, Pohutu, "the splasher," and the Prince of Wales' Feather being two of the most popular. Pohutu plays only at intervals, occasionally requiring a little soap to coax it, and a Moari, keepers always a shrill whistle some time before and so that visitors in the town can hurriedly betake themselves in the scene. The two most famous guides are the twin sisters, Georgina and Eileen, who are exactly alike, not only in their features and their raven locks, but also in the tattoo-marks that disfigure their mouth and chin. Thy speak English, as indeed do all educated Maoris, with a freedom from accent and a surprising elegance. The guide who conducted me, Bella, was free from tattoo-marks, and might have been taken for an Englishwoman with a strain of Southern blood. Her hut was like a museum of Antipodean curiosities and Occidental souvenirs, for side by side with grotesque wooden carvings and the "piupiu" or dancing-skirt of flaxen reads, it contained photographs and gifts of various kinds from Englishmen and Americans, whom she had conducted over her native heath. The entrance to her habitation was adorned by some forbidding figures carved in rata wood, who I understood represented some of her ancestors. She explained some of the symbolism that underlies the grim, barbaric designs in Maori art, such as the outstretched tongue of defiance that marks the warrior, but hinted at more than she alusidated, parrying the curiosity of the stranger with a graceful shyness. She led me through this Maori domain with an air of pride, showing me how her people cooked their food over the hot springs and washed their clothes in the hot pools, in which/at night or at dawn they also bathed.
